Local Estimation of Quantum Observables

A Review of Measurement Strategies and Sample Complexity

Reviews
Classical Shadows
Published

January 20, 2026

Abstract

Estimating expectation values of quantum observables is a fundamental task in quantum computing and quantum many-body physics. This review examines local measurement strategies for estimating both linear properties \mathrm{tr}(O\rho) and non-linear properties \mathrm{tr}(O\rho^2) of quantum states. The analysis is organized by operator structure: product observables, low-rank operators, and sums of Pauli operators. For each class, the discussion covers single-copy and multi-copy measurement protocols, derandomization techniques, and known complexity lower bounds. The review highlights the fundamental trade-offs between circuit depth and sample complexity, providing a unified perspective on classical shadow methods and their variants.

Introduction

Problem Statement

Consider a quantum system described by an n-qubit density matrix \rho. Two fundamental estimation problems arise in quantum information processing:

Linear Estimation Problem. Given an arbitrary operator O, determine the optimal sample complexity for estimating \mathrm{tr}(O\rho) under local measurement constraints.

Non-linear Estimation Problem. Given an arbitrary operator O, determine the optimal sample complexity for estimating \mathrm{tr}(O\rho^2) under local measurement constraints.

A central question is whether multi-copy measurement strategies can provide advantages over single-copy protocols when restricted to local operations.

Motivation and Applications

These estimation problems are motivated by several important applications:

  1. Variational Quantum Algorithms. Variational quantum eigensolvers (VQE) and related algorithms require efficient estimation of Hamiltonian expectation values  [1].

  2. Quantum Error Mitigation. Virtual distillation and related error mitigation schemes rely on estimating non-linear properties such as \mathrm{tr}(O\rho^2)  [2].

  3. Quantum Fisher Information. Estimation of the quantum Fisher information, which characterizes the sensitivity of quantum states to parameter changes, can be decomposed into Pauli operator estimations  [3].

  4. Fundamental Limits. Understanding the sample complexity of local estimation reveals fundamental constraints on information extraction from quantum systems, particularly for topologically ordered states where certain information is intrinsically non-local.

Notation

Throughout this review, the following notation is employed:

  • \mathcal{P}_n = \{I, X, Y, Z\}^{\otimes n}: the n-qubit Pauli group
  • \mathrm{wt}(P): the Pauli weight (number of non-identity tensor factors) of P \in \mathcal{P}_n
  • \|O\|_\infty: the operator norm (largest singular value) of O
  • \mathrm{SWAP}: the two-qubit swap operator

Preliminaries

Measurement Models

Two measurement paradigms are distinguished:

Single-copy (1-replica) measurements. Each measurement is performed on a single copy of \rho. The measurement outcome is used to construct an unbiased estimator of the target quantity.

Multi-copy (k-replica) measurements. Measurements are performed jointly on k copies of \rho, potentially with entangling operations between copies. This framework includes Bell measurements (k=2) and more general collective protocols.

The constraint of local measurements restricts operations to act on individual qubits (or small subsystems) without long-range entanglement within a single copy.

Classical Shadows Framework

The classical shadow formalism  [1] provides a unified approach to observable estimation. Given an ensemble of random unitaries \{U_i\} and measurement outcomes \{b_i\}, a classical shadow is constructed as: \hat{\rho} = \mathbb{E}_{U,b}[\mathcal{M}^{-1}(U^\dagger |b\rangle\langle b| U)] where \mathcal{M} is the measurement channel. For local Clifford measurements, this approach achieves sample complexity O(3^k) for weight-k Pauli observables  [4].

Robust variants of classical shadows  [5] address the challenge of noise in practical implementations.

Linear Observable Estimation

Product Observables

Definition. A product observable takes the form O = A_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes A_n where each A_i acts on a single qubit.

Diagonalizable Case

When each local operator satisfies [A_i, A_i^\dagger] = 0 (i.e., A_i is normal), the estimation problem is straightforward. One measures in the eigenbasis of each A_i at every position. For instance, if A_i \in \{I, X, Y, Z\}, this corresponds to direct Pauli measurement of \mathrm{tr}(P\rho).

Sample Complexity. The single-copy local strategy is optimal, requiring O(1/\epsilon^2) samples for \epsilon-precision estimation.

Non-diagonalizable Case

When [A_i, A_i^\dagger] \neq 0 for some positions, the operators cannot be simultaneously diagonalized. Applications include:

  • Estimation of creation/annihilation operators a^\dagger, a in bosonic sampling
  • Non-Hermitian Hamiltonian dynamics H + i\delta

Approaches:

  1. Cartesian decomposition: Decompose A = (A + A^\dagger)/2 + i(A - A^\dagger)/(2i) into Hermitian parts. However, non-commutativity leads to exponential growth in measurement bases.

  2. Classical shadow estimation: Applicable for local and low-rank cases with polynomial overhead  [1].

  3. Two-replica strategy: Bell measurements can estimate \{|\mathrm{tr}(P\rho)|\}_{P} with constant additive error using O(n) copies  [6].

Low-rank Observables

Definition. An observable O is low-rank if \mathrm{rank}(O) = r for some r \ll 2^n. The special case O = |\psi\rangle\langle\psi| corresponds to fidelity estimation.

Efficient Strategies:

  1. Stabilizer states: When |\psi\rangle is a stabilizer state with stabilizer group \mathcal{S}, the decomposition |\psi\rangle\langle\psi| = 2^{-n}\sum_{P \in \mathcal{S}} P enables efficient Pauli measurement.

  2. Entanglement witness construction: For a general observable O, one can examine O' = O + \alpha I such that O' is separable, analogous to entanglement witness construction.

  3. Bell difference sampling: This technique efficiently estimates the average over all stabilizer states  [6].

Sum of Pauli Operators

Definition. A Pauli decomposition takes the form O = \sum_{P \in \mathcal{P}_n} \alpha_P P.

Randomized Methods (Classical Shadows)

For single-copy local Clifford random measurements, the sample complexity scales as  [1]:

  • O(3^k/\epsilon^2) for weight-k Pauli observables
  • O(4^n/\epsilon^2) for arbitrary n-local operators

Two-copy variants:

  • Entanglement-fixed 2-copy shadow  [7]: Information-complete if entanglement is not maximal. Achieves efficiency O(3^{k/2}) for compatible weight-k Pauli observables.

  • Bell sampling: Informationally efficient for all Pauli operators  [6], though the signal problem may require additional samples  [8].

A fundamental lower bound establishes that single-replica estimation of all Pauli operators requires exponential sample complexity  [6].

Derandomized Methods

(1) Biased Sampling Methods

Instead of uniform random Clifford sampling, these methods adjust the measurement distribution based on target Hamiltonian structure:

  • Locally-biased shadows  [9]: For each qubit position, the local Clifford sampling distribution is biased according to Pauli weights in the Hamiltonian. This reduces variance for observables with structured Pauli decompositions.

  • Adaptive Pauli shadows  [10]: Combines classical computation with iterative distribution refinement, improving efficiency for molecular Hamiltonians.

(2) Greedy Derandomization

  • Iterative greedy selection  [11]: Systematically replaces random measurements with deterministic ones. For estimating L Pauli observables, achieves O(\log L) sample complexity by greedily selecting measurement bases that maximize information gain. (See Derandomized local shadows for details.)

(3) Commuting Pauli Grouping

These methods partition Pauli operators into simultaneously measurable groups:

  • Minimum Clique Cover  [12]: Maps the qubit-wise commuting (QWC) problem to graph coloring. Pauli operators form vertices with edges connecting non-commuting pairs.

  • SORTED INSERTION  [13]: A heuristic exploiting Pauli weight information for efficient groupings with lower computational overhead.

  • Unitary Partitioning  [14]: General framework for commuting grouping with provable guarantees.

(4) Theoretical Perspectives

  • Channel co-diagonalization  [15]: Seeks a quantum channel \Lambda such that multiple observables are simultaneously diagonalized.

  • Lower bounds  [16]: Establishes fundamental efficiency limits for local estimation with shallow circuits.

Non-linear Property Estimation

Purity and State Moments

The purity \mathrm{tr}(\rho^2) quantifies the mixedness of a quantum state. More generally, state moments \mathrm{tr}(\rho^k) characterize the eigenvalue distribution of \rho and appear in:

  • Rényi entropy estimation: S_\alpha(\rho) = \frac{1}{1-\alpha}\log\mathrm{tr}(\rho^\alpha)
  • Virtual distillation protocols  [2]
  • Entanglement quantification

Pauli-weighted Purity

Definition. For P \in \mathcal{P}_n, the Pauli-weighted purity is \mathrm{tr}(P\rho^2).

When A_i \in \mathrm{SWAP} \cdot \{I, X, Y, Z\}, the operator \mathrm{SWAP} \cdot P is non-Hermitian but normal (satisfying [SP, (SP)^\dagger] = 0), hence diagonalizable.

NoteTwo-copy Local Estimation of \mathrm{tr}(P\rho^2)

The value \mathrm{tr}(P\rho^2) can be estimated by a 2-copy local circuit:

  1. Apply \mathrm{CNOT}_{12} between corresponding qubits
  2. Measure Z on the second qubit with result s_1
  3. Adaptively apply S \cdot H gate if s_1 = 1, then measure Z on the first qubit with result s_2
  4. Construct estimator \hat{o} = \mathrm{Re}\left[\prod_k i^{2s_2^{(k)} + s_1^{(k)}}\right]
NoteProof

Full-weight Pauli operators can be locally transformed to Z^{\otimes n} using local Clifford gates (HXH = Z, HS^\dagger YSH = Z).

The observable becomes O = [(Z \otimes I) \cdot \mathrm{SWAP}]^{\otimes n} = A^{\otimes n}. The local operator A, though non-Hermitian, is normal and admits the spectral decomposition:

\begin{align} A &= |00\rangle\langle00| - |11\rangle\langle11| + i|\Phi^+\rangle\langle\Phi^+| - i|\Phi^-\rangle\langle\Phi^-| \end{align}

where |\Phi^\pm\rangle = (|01\rangle \pm i|10\rangle)/\sqrt{2}.

Measurement in the basis \{|00\rangle, |11\rangle, |\Phi^+\rangle, |\Phi^-\rangle\} yields outcomes \hat{o}_i \in \{+1, -1, +i, -i\}. Both \mathrm{Im}(\prod_i \hat{o}_i) and \mathrm{Re}(\prod_i \hat{o}_i) are bounded, so Hoeffding’s inequality ensures efficient estimation.

The circuit implementation uses: \mathrm{CNOT}|00\rangle = |00\rangle, \quad \mathrm{CNOT}|11\rangle = |10\rangle, \quad \mathrm{CNOT}|\Phi^\pm\rangle = (SH|0/1\rangle)|1\rangle

Limitation. Purity cannot be simultaneously estimated from outcomes \mathbf{s}_1, \mathbf{s}_2 because \mathrm{SWAP}|\Phi^+\rangle = i|\Phi^-\rangle.

As noted in  [2]:

“The inability to parallelize the measurement of commuting multi-qubit observables would make it challenging to profitably combine this approach with sophisticated NISQ measurement strategies. In particular, individual multi-qubit operators must be measured separately using this approach, even if they commute.”

Multi-copy Strategies

Classical Shadow-based Approaches

Single-replica bounds:

  • Unitary 6-design measurements achieve the lower bound \Omega(2^{n/2} \cdot \ln|\mathcal{O}|) for estimating \{\mathrm{tr}(P\rho^2)\}_{P \in \mathcal{O}}  [17].

Multi-replica constructions:

  • A k-replica strategy constructing classical shadows for \rho^t exists, with explicit construction for t=2 using non-local circuits  [18].

  • Local 2-copy 3-design shadow (details): Information-complete with sampling advantages over Bell sampling in specific regimes for weighted purity and non-linear Pauli properties.

  • Entanglement-fixed 2-copy shadow (details): Information-complete only when entanglement is non-maximal.

  • Random shifted Bell sampling  [7]: Information-incomplete but achieves O(n) sample complexity for \mathrm{tr}(O\rho^2).

Hybrid and Learning-based Methods

The hybrid framework  [19] combines classical and quantum resources for simulating many-body dynamics with improved efficiency.

Machine learning approaches  [20] demonstrate provably efficient estimation for certain classes of quantum many-body properties using classical shadow data.

Complexity Lower Bounds

Two-replica hardness. Even with non-local operations allowed and fixed operator O, the sample complexity is \Omega(2^{k/2}) where k is the support size  [17]  [21].

Conjectures:

Based on the observation that all known local 2-replica shadow protocols exhibit exponential sampling complexity, estimation of \{\mathrm{tr}(P\rho^2)\} for all P \in \mathcal{P}_n is conjectured to be hard for 2-replica strategies.

A 4-replica non-local upper bound exists for estimating \{\mathrm{tr}(P\rho^2)\} for all P \in \mathcal{P}_n, suggesting that 4-replica local estimation may also be fundamentally limited.

Open Questions and Outlook

Several important questions remain open:

ImportantOpen Question 1

If two-replica local measurement is allowed, can the exponential sampling complexity barrier for all Pauli observables be overcome?

ImportantOpen Question 2

For non-linear estimation \mathrm{tr}(O\rho^2), does there exist an optimal derandomization scheme under two-replica local constraints?

Partial results. Bell measurements can efficiently estimate observables of the form: O = \alpha_{00} I \otimes I + \alpha_{11} X \otimes X + \alpha_{22} Y \otimes Y + \alpha_{33} Z \otimes Z with \|O\|_\infty \leq O(1).

Future directions:

  1. Tight characterization of the sample complexity gap between single-copy and multi-copy protocols
  2. Development of adaptive measurement strategies that interpolate between randomized and deterministic approaches
  3. Extension of lower bound techniques to broader classes of non-linear properties
  4. Connections to quantum computational complexity and the role of entanglement in local estimation
